back: Data Structures and Algorithms — how you store data and the step-by-step methods to solve problems with it.
A way to organize data so common operations (look up, insert, delete) are fast.
A clear, finite set of steps that solves a problem.
A reusable problem shape (like “two pointers” or “hash map”) that many different questions share.
A short coding exercise you rewrite from memory until the pattern feels automatic.
A rule that stays true after every step of your loop — if you break it, the answer is wrong.
Try every possibility until you find the answer — correct but usually slow.
The best-known approach for speed (and sometimes space) on that problem type.
The official or community explanation of how to solve a problem.
A skeleton version of a pattern you fill in for each new problem.
What the function receives (array, string, number, etc.).
What you must return (value, index, boolean, count, or a changed array).
Change the given array without making a new one — usually saves memory.
Items sitting next to each other with no gaps in between.
A contiguous slice of an array (e.g. [2,3] inside [1,2,3,4]).
Items picked in order but not necessarily next to each other (e.g. [1,3] from [1,2,3]).
A contiguous piece of a string.
Characters kept in order but with characters in between allowed to be skipped.
Reads the same forward and backward ("racecar").
Two strings with the same letters in a different order ("listen" / "silent").
Arranged in increasing (or decreasing) order.
The same value appearing more than once.
The number or value you are trying to match, reach, or sum to.
Position of an element in an array (usually starting at 0).
Unusual but valid input (empty array, one element, all same values).
A limit on input size or what you are allowed to do (e.g. “no extra array”).
A fixed-order list of items accessed by position (index).
A flexible-length view of a sequence (Go’s dynamic array).
A sequence of characters.

front: What is Hash map / hash table?
back: A lookup table that finds a key’s value in roughly constant average time.
Same idea as a hash map — store key → value pairs.
A collection that only tracks whether each value is present (no duplicates).
Last-in, first-out — like a stack of plates; push on top, pop from top.
First-in, first-out — like a line; add at back, remove from front.
A queue where you can add or remove from both ends.
A structure that always gives you the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) item quickly.
Each node has at most two children: left and right.
A binary tree where left child < node < right child — enables fast search.
Nodes (vertices) connected by edges — models relationships and paths.
A graph stored as “each node → list of neighbors.”
A graph stored as a 2D table of which pairs are connected.
A 2D array of rows and columns (common in graph-as-grid problems).
Nodes chained by pointers; each node holds a value and a link to the next.
A tree built for fast prefix lookups on strings (like an autocomplete index).
How the number of steps grows as input size n grows.
How much extra memory your solution uses as n grows.
An upper bound — “at most about this slow” in the worst case.
A lower bound — “at least this slow.”
A tight bound — grows at exactly that rate (both upper and lower).
Constant time — work does not grow with n (e.g. hash lookup average case).
Logarithmic — each step cuts the problem in half (binary search, balanced tree height).
Linear — one pass through the data.
Common for efficient sorting and divide-and-conquer (e.g. merge sort).
Quadratic — nested loops over n (e.g. check every pair).
Exponential — choices branch wildly (naive recursion without memo).
Average cost per operation over many operations (e.g. dynamic array push is O(1) amortized).
Slowest possible input for your algorithm.
Typical random input behavior.
How many nested function calls stack up — counts toward space.
Using more memory to save time, or vice versa.
Walk through the array one element at a time.
Swap elements from both ends moving inward until the array is backward.
Use left and right indices to swap pairs while moving toward the center.

front: What is Running sum / prefix sum?
back: Cumulative total up to each index ([1,2,3] → [1,3,6]).
Sum of all elements from the start up to (and sometimes including) index i.
Move elements circularly — last items wrap to the front.
Remainder after division; used to wrap indices safely (e.g. k % n for rotation).
Turn a key into a table slot for fast lookup.
Store values seen so far; check if target - current already exists (two-sum trick).
The other number needed to reach a target (target - x).

front: What is Frequency map / frequency table?
back: Count how many times each key appears.
“Have I seen this value before?” — answered quickly with a set or map.
A normalized form used to group equivalent items (sorted letters for anagrams).
Two different keys landing in the same hash slot — handled by the map implementation.
Update a hash in O(1) when a window slides by adding/removing one element.
Two indices moving through data to enforce a rule without nested loops.
left at start, right at end — move inward (palindrome, container area).
read scans everything; write marks where the next kept value goes (compact in-place).
A contiguous range [left…right] that grows or shrinks to satisfy a condition.
Window size stays at k; slide by adding one right element and removing one left.
Window size changes — expand right until invalid, then shrink left until valid again.
The condition your window must satisfy (e.g. “sum ≤ 10”, “all unique chars”).
Track best subarray sum by choosing “extend current run” vs “start fresh here.”
Repeatedly guess the middle of a sorted range and discard the half that cannot contain the answer.
The range of indices or values you still consider possible.
First position where a condition becomes true (first index ≥ target).
First position where a condition would stop being true (past the last match).
Index where target would sit if inserted into sorted order.
A sorted array cut and shifted — one half is still sorted; binary search picks which half.
In a rotated array, one side of mid is fully sorted — use that to decide where to search.
Low bound, high bound, and middle index of the current search range.
One item in a tree with a value and links to children.
The top node of a tree — no parent above it.
A node with no children.
A node plus all descendants below it.
Longest path from a node down (height) or from root to a node (depth).
Visiting every node in a defined order.
Left subtree → current node → right subtree (gives sorted order in a BST).
Current node → left → right (copy tree shape).
Left → right → current node (delete or evaluate bottom-up).
Visit row by row top to bottom — usually done with a queue (BFS on a tree).
A function that calls itself on smaller subproblems (natural for trees).
The runtime’s stack of active function calls — simulated with an explicit stack when iterating.
Last in, first out — stack discipline.
Every closing bracket matches the most recent unmatched opener — classic stack use.
Stack kept in increasing or decreasing order to answer “next greater/smaller” in one pass.
For each position, the first warmer/larger value to its right.
Build the answer from answers to smaller subproblems, reusing work instead of recomputing.
A smaller version of the main question (e.g. “best up to index i”).
What one DP entry represents — always define in plain English first (dp[i] = …).
Smallest subproblems with known answers (e.g. n = 0 or n = 1).
Rule to compute a state from previous states.
Fill a table from small indices to large using loops.
Recurse with a cache so each subproblem is solved once.
At each step, choose include current item or exclude it (house robber pattern).
States depend on a single index along a line (array, stairs, costs).
States depend on two dimensions (two strings, grid paths).
Same subquestion asked many times — signal to use DP.
One point in a graph.
A connection between two nodes.
Edges have direction (A → B but not necessarily B → A).
Edges work both ways.
Each edge has a cost or distance.
A node directly connected by one edge.
Number of edges touching a node.
A group of nodes reachable from each other.
One connected blob of “land” cells in a grid metaphor.
Explore as far as possible along one path before backtracking.
Explore layer by layer — queue-based; finds shortest steps in unweighted graphs.

front: What is Visited set / visited array?
back: Marks cells or nodes already explored so you do not loop forever.
Recolor a connected region starting from one cell (paint-bucket idea).
Fewest edges between two nodes — BFS gives this on grids.
Move up, down, left, right on a grid.
A path that returns to a node already on the path.
Order nodes so every edge goes from earlier to later (task dependency order).
A complete binary tree stored in an array where parent is always ≤ children (min) or ≥ (max).
Smallest element is always at the top — good for “kth largest” by keeping only k items.
Largest element at the top — good for “take two biggest” simulations.
Abstract idea: always extract the highest- or lowest-priority item — heaps implement this.

front: What is Kth largest / kth smallest?
back: The element that would sit at position k if the array were sorted.
Partition array like quicksort but only recurse into the half containing k — average O(n).

front: What is Merge k sorted lists?
back: Repeatedly pick the smallest front element among k lists — classic min-heap use.
Try a choice, recurse, then undo the choice and try the next option.
Any combination of elements (include or exclude each).
Every ordering of all elements.
Choose exactly k items from n without caring about order.
One choice path in the search tree (include vs exclude, pick next number).
Stop exploring a branch early when it cannot lead to a valid answer.
Current list of choices built so far before backtracking.
Tree of all choices — backtracking walks it without visiting every node blindly.
Largest number that divides both a and b evenly.
Smallest positive number divisible by both a and b.
Repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0 — fast GCD.
Remainder after division; keeps numbers bounded in competitive problems.
Compute a^n mod m fast by squaring and multiplying only needed bits.
Number of ways to choose k items from n without order.
Integer greater than 1 with no divisors other than 1 and itself.
A number like 1, 2, 4, 8 — exactly one bit set in binary.
Use &, `
Bitwise exclusive or — useful for “cancel pairs” and parity problems.
Make the locally best choice at each step hoping it leads to a global optimum.
Split problem in half, solve halves, combine results (merge sort, binary search).
Follow the problem’s rules step by step exactly as described.
Rearrange elements into order — often O(n log n) for comparison sorts.
Count occurrences when value range is small — can beat O(n log n).
Track which elements belong to the same group with fast merge and lookup.
Shortest path in a weighted graph with non-negative edges — uses a priority queue.
Linear ordering of DAG nodes respecting all edge directions.
Directed acyclic graph — no cycles; good for dependencies.
DP where state is a subset encoded as bits in an integer.

front: What is Meet in the middle?
back: Split input in half, enumerate both halves, combine — tames exponential blow-up.
What goes in, what comes out, and whether input is mutated.
Control flow only — loops, recursion, early returns — before details.
Walk one concrete example step by step with variable values.
State the time and space complexity after you understand the shape.
Label the code shape (hash complement, sliding window, monotonic stack, etc.).
Restate the problem in one plain sentence a beginner would understand.

front: When you read “contiguous”, what does it usually mean?
back: elements must be next to each other
